subtype_info: Ebola virus infection in multiple patients in Guinea
title: Unrecognized Ebola virus infection in Guinea: complexity of surveillance in a health crisis situation: case report
case_text:
On November 30, 2014: the AT s daughter, FT developed a fever over 40 C, diarrhea, vomiting and physical asthenia. She was admitted at the Donka ETC, tested positive for the ebola Zaire virus by RT-PCR. Unfortunately, she died 11 days later. In total, 72 individuals have been registered as contacts around them. They were followed, released after 2 negative PCR and none developed any symptoms related to ebola disease.
History 3: fear and promiscuity: AB, 25 years old and his friend ZM 33 years old, are living in the same bedroom.
On March 26, 2015: AB: developed a fever associated with headache, dyspnea, joint pain and physical asthenia. After five days, he has been seen by a physician in cardiology department in an university hospital in Conakry. He received as an outpatient antimalarial treatment, antibiotics and anti-inflammatory. Given the persistence of signs, he has been seen by a traditional healer without success. Frightened by the epidemic context, he decided to hide to the contact tracing team. He has been finally located on April 17, 2015; he was asymptomatic. In Donka ETC, he has been tested positive for ebola Zaire by RT-PCR took care there and released after 2 negative consecutive RT-PCR. His friend ZM presented April 3, 2015 a fever, headache and joint pain. He has been admitted to Donka ETC with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Tested positive for ebola virus by RT-PCR. After treatment, he recovered. A total of 36 contacts have been registered monitored and released after 2 negatives PCR and none of them developed any symptoms related to ebola disease.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Ebola virus infection in multiple patients in Guinea
